content:
In a new study, Apple researchers have detailed SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model capable of generating both protein sequences and structures simultaneously. Details below.

Some background

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled "SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Simpler Than You Think," detailing a simplified method for predicting three-dimensional protein structures from amino acid sequences.

In short, SimpleFold uses a flow matching model to directly generate three-dimensional protein structures from amino acid sequences.

We've previously explained flow matching in detail, but in short, this technique starts from a noisier random point and learns a relatively direct path to the final result. This contrasts with diffusion models, which typically arrive at the final output through repeated denoising.

These two techniques are most commonly (or at least historically) associated with image generation, though researchers (including Apple's) have also explored applying diffusion models to text and code generation.

Returning to SimpleFold, Apple essentially combined flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (commonly used in text generation), allowing the model to bypass some of the more computationally expensive techniques typically used in protein folding models (such as DeepMind's famous AlphaFold).

Now, Apple researchers have introduced SimpleDesign, applying the pursuit of simpler, more general-purpose architectural concepts explored in SimpleFold to the broader protein design problem—not merely predicting three-dimensional protein structures.

SimpleDesign

As Apple researchers explained in a new study titled "SimpleDesign: A Unified Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Co-Design":

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on multi-stage pipelines, SimpleDesign learns to simultaneously generate amino acid sequences and continuous three-dimensional structures within a single end-to-end training process.

Many existing protein co-design models operate as follows: First, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations, or so-called "tokens." Then, they train a generative model to process these representations to generate new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips this intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequences and three-dimensional coordinates, rather than first compressing protein structures into a separate tokenized representation.

Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign in a rather interesting way.

They started with over 2 million protein sequence-structure pairs, primarily from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold database with other samples.

During training, they perturbed both parts of each data pair: amino acids in the sequence were randomly masked behind mask tokens, while the corresponding three-dimensional structures had noise added.

The researchers also adjusted the degree of perturbation on both sides. If the sequence was largely complete but the structure heavily corrupted, the task resembled protein folding, requiring the model to recover the structure from a known sequence.

Conversely, if the structure was largely complete but the sequence heavily masked, this resembled inverse folding. At this point, the model had to generate a sequence capable of producing the given structure.

And when both were partially perturbed, the model learned to handle both problems simultaneously, effectively training for protein co-design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign achieved competitive results on benchmarks including protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation, despite a significantly simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign can generate reasonable protein structures, and the amino acid sequences it produces are overall no worse than—and in some cases better than—those generated by most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign's results are currently limited to in-silico evaluations, as the generated proteins have not yet been experimentally tested to confirm whether they can actually fold, function, or operate safely in real biological systems.

Nonetheless, the results are quite encouraging, and the entire study (which naturally explores SimpleDesign's architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results in much greater depth) is well worth reading.
